title: Cappadocian Greek, with Pharasa and Sille: Greek under Turkish influence
lead: Until 1923 Greek was spoken in three islands of speech deep inside Anatolia: a group of villages in **Cappadocia** (around Kayseri and Niğde), **Pharasa** and six villages in its valley to the east, and the single village of **Sille** near Konya. After nine centuries of contact with Turkish, these dialects changed more than any other form of Greek: they took Turkish vowels, vowel harmony, endings stacked one after another, and often lost grammatical gender. Nikolaos Kontosopoulos wrote that a reader of Cappadocian 'cannot tell whether it is Turkish in a Greek mouth or Greek in a Turkish mouth'. It was thought extinct by the 1960s, until in 2005 linguists found fluent speakers of the Mistiot variety in Greece.
facts: Before 1923: Mistí, Malakopí, Anakú, Axó, Aravaní, Ulağaç, Potamiá, Delmesó, Sinasós and other villages; Pharasa (Çamlıca near Yahyalı); Sille (near Konya, ancient Iconium). After 1923: refugee villages in central and northern Greece.

A small number of mostly older and middle-aged speakers of **Μιστιώτικα** (Mistiot), found by Mark Janse and Dimitris Papazachariou in 2005; Pharasiot has been described from speakers in Greece as recently as 2018.
Byzantine Greek of central Anatolia, cut off after the Battle of Manzikert (1071) and the Seljuk conquest.
Unwritten for most of its history; recorded by scholars from the 19th c. on, often with extra letters (**σ̌, ζ̌, τσ̌**) and Turkish vowels (ı, ö, ü).
Many Orthodox Christians of the area spoke only Turkish (the **Καραμανλήδες**, who wrote Turkish in Greek letters).

timeline.text: The old Anatolian languages die out and central Anatolia becomes Greek-speaking. Cappadocia gives Byzantium emperors (Maurice, Heraclius) and Church Fathers (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa).

After the defeat at **Manzikert**, Seljuk Turks take central Anatolia. Cappadocian starts to develop apart from the rest of Greek, and is never touched by the Venetian and French influence of the later Frankokratia.
The earliest written traces: a few lines of Greek in the macaronic poems of **Jalal ad-Din Rumi** (1207–1273) in Konya and his son Sultan Walad, written in Arabic script.
Many Christian communities shift to Turkish. Greek holds on in villages around Kayseri and Niğde, in Pharasa and in Sille, but changes under intense bilingualism.
**R. M. Dawkins** does fieldwork; his *Modern Greek in Asia Minor* (1916) remains the classic description of Sille, Cappadocia and Pharasa.
The population exchange moves all Orthodox Christians to Greece. Children are encouraged to switch to Standard Greek; the dialect retreats into families.
Janse and Papazachariou find Mistiot speakers in central and northern Greece; revival work, a documentary (*Last Words*) and social-media groups follow.

sections.after: The vowel-harmony verbs show how deep the contact went: the Greek verb ending **-ίζω** takes the vowel of the Turkish stem (Turkish *istemek, anlamak, oturmak, düşünmek*), just as Turkish suffixes do.

sections.h: Nouns: animacy, endings in a row, and lost gender
sections.text: Cappadocian nouns behave in ways no other Greek does. Animate and inanimate nouns decline differently, endings are added one after another as in Turkish, and in most of Cappadocia (much less in Sille) grammatical gender has almost disappeared: a woman can be **το ναίκα**. In south-western varieties such as Ulağaç, every noun takes the neuter article **do / da** and neuter adjectives. A definite direct object is marked by a different form from an indefinite one, again as in Turkish.

sections.after: Word order is governed by topic and focus, but tends towards Turkish **subject–object–verb**. Turkish idioms were translated word for word: 'he did it himself' is **οπ σ̌έριν dου τα ποίκι**, 'he did it with his own hand'.

sections.text: Cut off before the Crusades, Cappadocian kept Byzantine and ancient words where the standard took Italian or new Greek ones.

notes: **Pharasiot** (Φάρασα and the villages of its valley) had the least Turkish influence of the three, more Armenian loanwords, and kept forms without synizesis (**μαλία, χωρίο** for **μαλλιά, χωριό**). Stressed ι can become [ie] (**λιέγο, διέχνω** for **λίγο, δείχνω**); final -ς drops before **μου** (**ο dada μου** 'my father', but **ο dadas**). Some scholars place it closer to Pontic than to Cappadocian.

**Silliot** (Σίλλη, near Konya) was the most divergent of all. Its σ is always [ʃ], θ became σ (**σύρα** for **θύρα** 'door'), δ became ρ (**ρώρεκα** for **δώδεκα**), τ became [tʃ] before ι (**ότσ̌ι** for **ότι**). It kept gender better than Cappadocia proper.

sections.h: Why did Cappadocian change so much?
sections.text: Three conditions came together: very long separation from other Greek (from the 11th century), a small number of speakers in each village, and **universal bilingualism** with Turkish, the language of the state, the market and often the home. Linguists use Cappadocian as a textbook case of how far 'borrowing' can go: not just words, but sounds, word order and even the shape of endings (Thomason & Kaufman 1988). R. M. Dawkins summed it up in his often-quoted remark that in these dialects 'the body has remained Greek, but the soul has become Turkish'. Recent research (Karatsareas, Janse) shows that much of the change, such as the loss of gender, also follows inner Greek tendencies that Turkish contact accelerated.

sample.intro: Kontosopoulos's description, from his survey of the dialects, and the Turkish-model idiom quoted by Dawkins.
lines: «Όποιος ακούει (ή μάλλον διαβάζει) την καππαδοκική διάλεκτο, δεν ξέρει αν έχει να κάνει με τουρκικά σε ελληνικό στόμα ή με ελληνικά σε στόμα τούρκικο.»
en: 'Whoever hears (or rather reads) the Cappadocian dialect cannot tell whether it is Turkish in a Greek mouth or Greek in a Turkish mouth.'
'He did it with his own hand', i.e. he did it himself: a Turkish idiom in Greek words.
sample.source: Κοντοσόπουλος 1994: 7, quoted on the Portal for the Greek Language; Dawkins 1916: 198–199.

questions.q: What event cut Cappadocia off from the rest of the Greek world?
questions.why: The Seljuk conquest of central Anatolia followed it.
A feminine noun takes the neuter article; in Ulağaç every noun does.

questions.q: Why does the verb ending change in **ανλαdə́ζω** vs **οτουρdούζω**?
questions.why: The ending copies the vowel quality of the Turkish stem (anla-, otur-).

questions.q: Which old Greek word for 'door' survives in Cappadocian?
questions.why: Cappadocian θίρ / tír; the standard πόρτα comes from Italian.

questions.q: In which year were fluent Cappadocian speakers rediscovered in Greece?
questions.why: Mark Janse and Dimitris Papazachariou found Mistiot speakers in central and northern Greece.

gloss.ιστεντίζω: ιστεντίζω (Cappadocian, Turkish istemek) — I want = θέλω
gloss.λύκο: λύκο — wolf (acc.); in Cappadocian the definite object form
gloss.λυκι̯ού: λυκιού (Cappadocian) — of the wolf = του λύκου
gloss.φόβοζι̯α: φόβοζια (Cappadocian) — fears: plural by an added suffix
gloss.ι̯ου: -ιου (Cappadocian) — genitive suffix added to the noun
gloss.ναίκεζ: ναίκεζ-ιου (Cappadocian) — of the women = των γυναικών
gloss.ερχουμεστινιζ: ερχουμεστινιζ (Cappadocian) — we come = ερχόμαστε, with Turkish -iz
gloss.τον: τον — him (acc.); in Delmesó ήρτα τον 'I had come' (Turkish idi 'was')
gloss.εναίκας: ναίκα — woman; κουγιουμτζή εναίκας οντά = the goldsmith's wife's room
gloss.ποίκα: ποίκα (Cappadocian) — I did, from Byzantine έποικα
gloss.κάνει: κάνει — he does; Cappadocian 'it is enough' (ἱκανεῖ)
